claims.claim: The gain modulation can transfer between brain hemispheres.
claims.source: It involves a large local increase in contrast gain which spreads forward after a delay (e.g. an occlusion) and can even transfer between brain hemispheres, predicting trajectories moved towards the visual midline from the other eye.
claims.evidence: Shown by experiments where primers in one eye's visual field affect responses in the contralateral hemisphere (Figure 3C).

claims.claim: A diverse range of animals are capable of visually detecting moving objects within cluttered environments.
claims.source: A diverse range of animals are capable of visually detecting moving objects within cluttered environments.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement based on established scientific knowledge about animal vision.

claims.claim: Small target detection is a complex task, particularly in response to a small target generating very weak contrast as it moves against a highly textured background.
claims.source: This discrimination is a complex task, particularly in response to a small target generating very weak contrast as it moves against a highly textured background.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the physics of visual detection and established knowledge of visual processing challenges.

claims.claim: In the vertebrate retina, high initial gain combined with neuronal adaptation and sensitization allows responses from a network of overlapping ganglion cells to 'keep up' with the current target location and account for sluggish neuronal delays.
claims.source: In the vertebrate retina, high initial gain combined with neuronal adaptation and sensitization allows responses from a network of overlapping ganglion cells to 'keep up' with the current target location and account for sluggish neuronal delays (Berry et al., 1999; Kastner and Baccus, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research by Berry et al., 1999 and Kastner and Baccus, 2013.

claims.claim: Vertebrate retinal encoding anticipates targets moving in a straight line, with trajectory reversals eliciting a synchronous burst of activity from a population of ganglion cells.
claims.source: This encoding anticipates targets moving in a straight line, with trajectory reversals eliciting a synchronous burst of activity from a population of ganglion cells (Schwartz et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Schwartz et al., 2007 and Chen et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Vertebrate retinal anticipation does not use the recent trajectory to extrapolate likely target locations at future times.
claims.source: However, this anticipation does not use the recent trajectory to extrapolate likely target locations at future times.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a contrast to the dragonfly mechanism, based on understanding of vertebrate retinal processing from cited literature.

claims.claim: In vertebrate retina, the last observed location remains sensitized after the target disappears.
claims.source: Rather, the last observed location remains sensitized after the target disappears.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature on vertebrate retinal processing.

claims.claim: Human observers show improved sensitivity at the extrapolated forward location when a target is temporarily occluded.
claims.source: This differs from studies of human observers, where a temporarily occluded target results in improved sensitivity at the extrapolated forward location (Watamaniuk and McKee, 1995).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Watamaniuk and McKee, 1995.

claims.claim: Predictive encoding of future target locations indicates the presence of additional processing mechanisms beyond the retina.
claims.source: This predictive encoding of future target locations indicates the presence of additional processing mechanisms beyond the retina.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between retinal processing and human behavioral performance.

claims.claim: Dragonflies estimate target location, capturing single prey in visual clutter, even amidst a swarm of potential alternatives.
claims.source: Like human ball players, dragonflies also estimate target location, capturing single prey in visual clutter, even amidst a swarm of potential alternatives (Corbet, 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Corbet, 1999.

claims.claim: A 'winner-takes-all' neuron in the dragonfly likely subserves competitive selection of an individual target whilst ignoring a distracter.
claims.source: We recently described a 'winner-takes-all' neuron in the dragonfly likely to subserve such competitive selection of an individual target, whilst ignoring a distracter (Wiederman and O'Carroll, 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to the authors' prior work (Wiederman and O'Carroll, 2013).

claims.claim: In other animal models, inhibitory circuits drive the selection of salient stimuli.
claims.source: In other animal models, inhibitory circuits drive the selection of salient stimuli (Mysore and Knudsen, 2013) and the direction of attention towards targets is evidenced by modulation of contrast gain (Moran and Desimone, 1985; Reynolds et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mysore and Knudsen, 2013.

claims.claim: The direction of attention towards targets is evidenced by modulation of contrast gain.
claims.source: In other animal models, inhibitory circuits drive the selection of salient stimuli (Mysore and Knudsen, 2013) and the direction of attention towards targets is evidenced by modulation of contrast gain (Moran and Desimone, 1985; Reynolds et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Moran and Desimone, 1985 and Reynolds et al., 2000.

claims.claim: How prediction relates to the selection of salient stimuli is unknown.
claims.source: How prediction relates to the selection of salient stimuli is unknown (Zirnsak et al., 2014) and how selection, prediction and attention are encoded at the neuronal level is an intense topic of scientific investigation.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Zirnsak et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Small target-selective neurons in predatory dragonflies show local changes in sensitivity elicited during target tracking.
claims.source: Here we used intact, in vivo, recordings from the system of small target-selective neurons in predatory dragonflies to reveal local changes in sensitivity elicited during target tracking.
claims.evidence: This is the main experimental finding, supported by data throughout the Results section.

claims.claim: The local changes in sensitivity involve a large increase in contrast gain just ahead of the target's most recent location, with suppression in the surround.
claims.source: We show that this involves a large increase in contrast gain just ahead of the target's most recent location, with suppression in the surround.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 3 and 5.

claims.claim: A local increase in gain spreads forward after a delay.
claims.source: Our data shows that a local increase in gain spreads forward after a delay, even anticipating the path of primers presented to the contralateral eye and moved towards the visual midline.
claims.evidence: Shown by experiments with temporal delays (Figure 3B, Figure 4).

claims.claim: The direction tuning shifts to match the prior path.
claims.source: Moreover, the direction tuning shifts to match the prior path.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by direction selectivity experiments (Figure 6).

claims.claim: These response attributes differentiate this neuronal processing from typical models of direction selectivity.
claims.source: Such response attributes differentiate this neuronal processing from typical models of direction selectivity and are ideally suited for a dragonfly's predictive pursuit of prey (Mischiati et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with known models of direction selectivity and the observed data.

claims.claim: STMD neurons in the dragonfly Hemicordulia tau are tuned to target size and velocity and are highly sensitive to contrast.
claims.source: 'Small target motion detector' (STMD) neurons in the dragonfly, Hemicordulia tau, are tuned to target size and velocity and are highly sensitive to contrast (O'Carroll 1993, Wiederman et al., 2008, 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to O'Carroll 1993 and Wiederman et al., 2008, 2013.

claims.claim: CSTMD1 responds selectively to a small, moving target, even when embedded within natural scenes.
claims.source: One identified STMD, CSTMD1, responds selectively to a small, moving target, even when embedded within natural scenes (Wiederman and O'Carroll, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wiederman and O'Carroll, 2011.

claims.claim: CSTMD1 exhibits a sophisticated form of selective attention.
claims.source: CSTMD1 also exhibits a sophisticated form of selective attention.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subsequent description and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: CSTMD1 responds in a winner-takes-all manner when presented with two simultaneously moving targets, selecting a single target as if the distracter does not exist.
claims.source: Instead, CSTMD1 responds in a winner-takes-all manner, selecting a single target as if the distracter does not even exist (Wiederman and O'Carroll, 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wiederman and O'Carroll, 2013.

claims.claim: Long, continuous target trajectories reveal higher overall spiking activity compared to short trajectories at the same spatial locations.
claims.source: This reveals higher overall spiking activity in response to the long, continuous target trajectories.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by comparing Figure 1A and 1B.

claims.claim: Neuronal responses build slowly over hundreds of milliseconds, a property termed facilitation.
claims.source: We note that neuronal responses build slowly over hundreds of milliseconds - a property we have previously termed facilitation (Nordström et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Nordström et al., 2011 and observed in the data traces.

claims.claim: For the primer & probe condition, responses to the probe are facilitated compared to probe alone.
claims.source: For the primer & probe condition (where a primer always precedes the probe stimulus) responses to the probe are facilitated (green region, cf. black with blue time courses).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1C data traces.

claims.claim: The facilitatory effect is not simply due to slow kinetics, as both responses have a rapid decay time course when the stimulus ends.
claims.source: This facilitatory effect is not simply due to slow kinetics, as both responses have a rapid decay time course when the stimulus ends (Dunbier et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by observation of the data and citation to Dunbier et al., 2012.

claims.claim: CSTMD1's excitatory receptive field extends from the dorsal, visual midline to the periphery.
claims.source: These reveal CSTMD1's excitatory receptive field which extends from the dorsal, visual midline to the periphery.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claims.claim: In the other visual hemifield, a drifting target generates inhibition, with activity suppressed to below spontaneous levels.
claims.source: In the other visual hemifield (midline at 0° azimuth), a drifting target generates inhibition (Figure 1D,E), with activity suppressed to below spontaneous levels (0 spikes/s from a spontaneous activity of 11 ± 4 spikes/s, mean ± std.).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by data in Figure 1D and 1E.

claims.claim: A pronounced 'focus' of increased sensitivity exists just ahead of the final location of the priming target with an extensive region of suppression in surrounding locations.
claims.source: Figure 3A reveals a pronounced 'focus' of increased sensitivity just ahead of the final location of the priming target and an extensive region of suppression in surrounding locations (mean, n = 9 dragonflies).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 3A with statistical support (n=9 dragonflies).

claims.claim: There is over 50% increase in spike rate within the focus center and up to 50% decrease in surrounding locations.
claims.source: In Figure 3A, we observed a large mean change in spike rate – over 50% increase within the focus center (p=0.0007, n = 9) and up to 50% decrease in surrounding locations (p=0.005, n = 9).
claims.evidence: Quantified from Figure 3A data with statistical significance reported.

claims.claim: With a 300 ms delay after the primer, the focus spreads forward in spatial extent.
claims.source: If the primer disappears for 300 ms before each probe, a similarly intense focus is still evident (Figure 3B, Video 2), but now spread forward in spatial extent (p=0.005, n = 7 dragonflies).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3B with statistical support.

claims.claim: The focus accounts for the expected target location had it continued on its original trajectory.
claims.source: The focus seems to account for the expected target location had it continued on its original trajectory (to a position as indicated by the white cross-hair in Figure 3B,C), albeit with an increased uncertainty given its broader spatial extent (mean, n = 7 dragonflies).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial distribution of the focus shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The focus transfers across the brain to the ipsilateral hemisphere when a horizontal primer moves toward the visual midline in the contralateral eye.
claims.source: Moreover, if we move a horizontal primer toward the visual midline in the contralateral eye before it disappears for 300 ms, the focus transfers across the brain to the ipsilateral hemisphere (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The inter-hemispheric transfer cannot be explained by facilitation being regenerated in the ipsilateral eye because the stimulus avoided the binocular overlap region.
claims.source: Our stimulus was carefully designed to avoid this region, disappearing just before entering the area of overlap. Therefore, our result cannot be explained by facilitation being regenerated in the ipsilateral eye.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and knowledge of dragonfly visual anatomy.

claims.claim: The inter-hemispheric transfer must involve a localized, inter-hemispheric transfer of information.
claims.source: Rather it must involve a localized, inter-hemispheric transfer of information.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results and anatomical constraints.

claims.claim: A localized and spatially segregated combination of enhancement and suppression cannot be explained by a simple global mechanism such as post-inhibitory rebound.
claims.source: Furthermore, a localized and spatially segregated combination of enhancement and suppression (red and blue regions in Figure 3C) cannot be explained by a simple global mechanism, such as, a post-inhibitory rebound following a strong inhibitory stimulus (Bolzon et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial pattern of results and comparison with known mechanisms.

claims.claim: The transfer of a predictive focus between brain hemispheres is likely to play a crucial role in the prediction of target location during pursuit flights.
claims.source: This transfer of a predictive focus between brain hemispheres is likely to play a crucial role in the prediction of target location during pursuit flights where the pursuer attempts to fixate the target frontally (Mischiati et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and cited behavioral observations.

claims.claim: There is a forward shift in the focus region following an occlusion.
claims.source: There is a forward shift in the focus region (mean ± SEM, p=0.03, n = 12 dragonflies) following an occlusion (cf. 100 ms pause, yellow line with 300 ms pause, green line).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 3E with statistical support.

claims.claim: A small 6° jump backwards precisely over the previously primed path resets the response magnitude to that of the unfacilitated response.
claims.source: These data (mean ± SEM) show that a small (6°) jump backwards precisely over the previously primed path already resets the response magnitude to that of the unfacilitated response (dashed line), whilst larger jumps backwards (12°) reveal potent suppression.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 3E data.

claims.claim: The prior primer target exerts long-lasting effects on the surrounding receptive field.
claims.source: Considering that the largest jump in this case is stimulating a part of the receptive field that last saw the target up to 700 ms earlier, the profound inhibition seen for this stimulus suggests that the prior primer target exerts long-lasting effects on the surrounding receptive field.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal characteristics of the experiment and observed inhibition.

claims.claim: A small 4° instantaneous jump ahead of the primer leads to a response time course with a very rapid rise to a level similar to the fully facilitated state.
claims.source: The small 4° instantaneous jump ahead of the primer leads to a response time course with a very rapid rise to a level similar to the fully facilitated state (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: A 12° instantaneous jump elicits a similar response time course to the unfacilitated probe.
claims.source: However, a 12° instantaneous jump elicits a similar (slower) response time course to the unfacilitated probe (grey line), confirming the limited extent to which facilitation initially extends ahead of the target path.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4A and used to infer the spatial extent of facilitation.

claims.claim: A large 20° jump ahead bypassing the focus-region entirely reveals surround suppression.
claims.source: A large 20° jump ahead (Figure 4A) bypassing the focus-region entirely, again reveals surround suppression, with a much slower response time course than the control.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Instantaneous backwards jumps reveal potent suppression.
claims.source: Instantaneous backwards jumps (Figure 4B) also reveal potent suppression.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Facilitation strength slowly decays over time at the last seen location of the target.
claims.source: Pauses without a jump (0°), show that facilitation strength slowly decays over time at the last seen location of the target (Figure 4C,E, Cohen's d = 4.48).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4C and 4E with effect size reported.

claims.claim: With no pause, the strongest responses occur 4° in front of the moving target.
claims.source: With no pause (0 ms), the strongest responses occur 4° in front of the moving target (Figure 4E) as observed in the 2D receptive fields (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4E and consistent with Figure 3A.

claims.claim: When larger jumps are matched to their respective pauses as might be expected during trajectory occlusions, there is a statistically significant increase in the resultant spiking activity.
claims.source: When larger jumps are matched to their respective pauses as might be expected during trajectory occlusions (12° and 300 ms; 20° and 500 ms) there is a statistically significant increase in the resultant spiking activity (Figure 4E, Cohen's d = 2.0 and 2.32 respectively).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4E with statistical support and effect sizes.

claims.claim: Both low and high contrast primers induce a large increase in response, with a larger output range and a greater than 5-fold increase in contrast sensitivity.
claims.source: Both primers induced a large increase in response, with a larger output range (increased maximum response) and a greater than 5-fold increase in contrast sensitivity (Figure 5C, contrast threshold reduced from 0.071 to 0.013 for near threshold stimuli, C50 from 0.36 to 0.13, n = 9 dragonflies).
claims.evidence: Quantified from Figure 5C data.

claims.claim: Lower contrast primers induce less overall activity during the priming stimulus, yet their effect on subsequent responses is remarkably similar to high contrast primers.
claims.source: Lower contrast primers themselves induce less overall activity during the priming stimulus (Figure 5D, Cohen's d = 0.97), yet their effect on subsequent responses to stimuli presented at the expected location is remarkably similar to high contrast primers (cf. pink with red lines in Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: The gain modulation is not elicited solely by the stimulus contrast or the neuronal activity induced by the primer per se, but rather by target presence.
claims.source: This suggests that the gain modulation is not elicited solely by the stimulus contrast or the neuronal activity induced by the primer per se, but rather by target presence.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of effects from low and high contrast primers.

claims.claim: The gain modulation may indicate a 'switch' process rather than a simpler, activity-dependent gain control mechanism.
claims.source: This may indicate a 'switch' process, such as that suggested for neural circuits in the auditory brain stem of the barn owl (Mysore et al., 2011), rather than a simpler, activity-dependent gain control mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the data and comparison with other systems.

claims.claim: The boost of response gain is largest at mid-contrast, with softer saturation at high contrasts, extending the range of contrasts over which the response is modulated by a full order of magnitude.
claims.source: Another interesting feature of the facilitated contrast sensitivity is that the boost of response gain is largest at mid-contrast, with softer saturation at high contrasts, extending the range of contrasts over which the response is modulated by a full order of magnitude.
claims.evidence: Observed in the shape of the contrast sensitivity function in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The reduction in slope of the contrast sensitivity function would reduce overall response variance to changes in the contrast of the selected target.
claims.source: Moreover, the reduction in slope of the contrast sensitivity function would reduce overall response variance to changes in the contrast of the selected target, a phenomenon also observed in humans (Avidan et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the shape of the function, with comparison to human studies.

claims.claim: The increased contrast sensitivity is localized to the focus-region.
claims.source: Our results also show that the increased contrast sensitivity is localized to the focus-region evident in Figure 3.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by comparing local vs. distant primer effects in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: A more distant primer displaced 20° to the side of the probe does not evoke facilitation of the contrast sensitivity function.
claims.source: A more distant primer displaced 20° to the side of the probe does not evoke facilitation of the contrast sensitivity function (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 5C (yellow line).

claims.claim: Following a high contrast primer, the hyperpolarizing motion-after-effect reaches almost 4 mV and suppresses subsequent spiking activity for several hundred milliseconds.
claims.source: Following a high contrast primer, this hyperpolarizing motion-after-effect (MAE) reaches almost 4 mV and suppresses subsequent spiking activity for several hundred milliseconds (Figure 5D,E), an attenuation that may compete with spatially-localized facilitation.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claims.claim: Interaction between the facilitation time course and longer-term suppression with slow kinetics may be analogous to the 'inhibition of return' observed in human reaction time experiments.
claims.source: Interaction between the facilitation time course and longer-term suppression with slow kinetics may be analogous to the 'inhibition of return' observed in human reaction time experiments (Posner and Cohen, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on comparison with human behavioral phenomena.

claims.claim: CSTMD1 appears to be only weakly direction-selective when stimulated with targets moving along prolonged paths.
claims.source: The facilitated response of CSTMD1 appears to be only weakly direction-selective when stimulated with targets moving along prolonged paths.
claims.evidence: This is based on prior characterization and current observations.

claims.claim: Within each hemifield, CSTMD1 has a weak preference for progressive motion upwards and away from the midline.
claims.source: Within each hemifield, CSTMD1 has a weak preference for progressive motion upwards and away from the midline (rightwards for the neurons recorded here) (Nordström et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Nordström et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Probe responses alone are both weak and weakly direction selective.
claims.source: Probe responses alone are both weak and weakly direction selective (Figure 6C, grey dots).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: All four primers facilitate responses maximally in the direction of the primer's path, shifting the direction tuning to match that of the primer.
claims.source: But all four primers facilitate responses maximally in the direction of the primer's path, shifting the direction tuning to match that of the primer (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 6C polar plots.

claims.claim: The magnitude of facilitation is considerably larger in CSTMD1's weak preferred direction (upwards and rightwards).
claims.source: However, the magnitude of facilitation (Figure 6E) is considerably larger in CSTMD1's weak preferred, direction (upwards and rightwards for this hemisphere's CSTMD1).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Following a reversal of the target trajectory, CSTMD1's response is strongly inhibited compared to the corresponding probe alone response.
claims.source: Following a reversal of the target trajectory (Figure 6F, blue and purple lines), CSTMD1's response is strongly inhibited compared to the corresponding probe alone response (grey lines).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: The dragonfly response to trajectory reversals contrasts with findings in the vertebrate retina, where a subset of ganglion cells respond strongly and synchronously to motion reversals.
claims.source: This contrasts with findings in the vertebrate retina, where a subset of ganglion cells respond strongly and synchronously to motion reversals (Schwartz et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature.

claims.claim: Jumping the probe stimulus 4° forward into the predicted center of the focus region induces much weaker direction selectivity than probes that radiate away from the end of the same priming path.
claims.source: We tested this by jumping the probe stimulus 4° forward into the predicted center of the focus region (Figure 7A, Video 5). This stimulus induced much weaker direction selectivity (Figure 7B) than those that radiate away from the end of the same priming path (b1/b0 ratio of 0.32 vs. 0.50, p=0.04).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 7B with statistical support.

claims.claim: Probes that reverse direction relative to the primer are not facilitated, except when the probe jumps 4° into the focus center.
claims.source: Probes that reverse direction relative to the primer are not facilitated, except when the probe jumps 4° into the focus center (Figure 7C, Cohen's d = 3.90).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 7C with effect size reported.

claims.claim: The predictive focus of gain modulation is a spatial phenomenon, established by the past trajectory.
claims.source: Thus, the predictive focus of gain modulation is a spatial phenomenon, established by the past trajectory.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the experiments showing spatial localization of the effect.

claims.claim: The apparent direction selectivity induced by primers is not due to any change in the local bias of underlying motion detectors to any one stimulus direction, but rather from the overall displacement of the focus ahead of the target location.
claims.source: This suggests that the apparent direction selectivity induced by primers is not due to any change in the local bias of underlying motion detectors to any one stimulus direction, but rather from the overall displacement of the focus ahead of the target location.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of experiments with and without spatial jumps.

claims.claim: Direction selectivity is established even more rapidly than the gain in the facilitated response over a target's developing trajectory.
claims.source: Over a target's developing trajectory, direction selectivity (quantified here as vector magnitude) is established even more rapidly than the gain in the facilitated response (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The emergence of directional tuning raises the possibility that the modulation assists anticipation of target trajectories by promoting the expectation of a continued path.
claims.source: The emergence of directional tuning raises the intriguing possibility that the modulation assists anticipation of target trajectories - promoting the expectation of a continued path.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observed directional tuning.

claims.claim: Small-field STMDs are located at an earlier stage of visual processing than CSTMD1.
claims.source: We also tested for the facilitatory component of the predictive gain modulation in likely pre-cursor neurons: small-field (SF) STMDs located at an earlier stage of visual processing (Barnett et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Barnett et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Retinotopically organized SF-STMDs have inputs in the outer lobula, a region akin to mammalian primary visual cortex.
claims.source: Retinotopically organized SF-STMDs have inputs in the outer lobula, a region akin to mammalian primary visual cortex (Okamura and Strausfeld, 2007; O'Carroll 1993).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Okamura and Strausfeld, 2007 and O'Carroll 1993.

claims.claim: SF-STMDs have properties similar to end-stopped (hypercomplex) cells.
claims.source: They have properties similar to end-stopped (hypercomplex) cells (Nordström and O'Carroll, 2009), which are modulated by contextual stimuli presented outside their classical receptive field (Polat et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Nordström and O'Carroll, 2009 and Polat et al., 1998.

claims.claim: Primers moving toward the SF-STMD receptive field facilitate the probe responses by over 40%, whilst those heading away elicit no facilitation.
claims.source: Primers moving toward the receptive field facilitate the probe responses by over 40%, whilst those heading away elicit no facilitation.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claims.claim: Facilitation is observed in other large-field STMD neurons, with an average gain of over 80%.
claims.source: This predictive gain modulation may be inherited and improved downstream, since we also observe facilitation in other large-field STMD neurons, with an average gain of over 80% (Figure 8C, Cohen's d = 1.02).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 8C with effect size reported.

claims.claim: At least one identified SF-STMD axon traverses the brain with an output arborization located within a limited area of the contralateral lobula.
claims.source: Supporting this hypothesis, at least one identified (dye-filled) SF-STMD axon traverses the brain with an output arborization located within a limited area of the contralateral lobula (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 8E (morphological data).

claims.claim: SF-STMD neurons are perfectly suited for the spatially localized inter-hemispheric modulation, both excitatory and inhibitory.
claims.source: Neurons such as this are thus perfectly suited for the spatially localized inter-hemispheric modulation, both excitatory and inhibitory shown in Figure 3C.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomy and the functional observations.

claims.claim: A neuron's receptive field is a dynamic representation of the spatial and temporal context, not just stimulus selectivity.
claims.source: However, our results show that in addition to stimulus selectivity (contrast, size, velocity), a neuron's receptive field is also a dynamic representation of the spatial (Wiederman and O'Carroll, 2013) and temporal context.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Modulation of the dynamic receptive field represents anticipatory coding, a more complex influence of history than simple neuronal adaptation, sensitization, habituation or fatigue.
claims.source: Here modulation of the dynamic receptive field represents anticipatory coding, a more complex influence of history than simple neuronal adaptation, sensitization, habituation or fatigue.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of known neuronal mechanisms.

claims.claim: The 'omitted stimulus response' in the vertebrate retina is an example of complexity in processing where an omitted component of a periodic pattern predictively elicits robust neuronal activity.
claims.source: Indeed, such complexity in processing is also evident in the 'omitted stimulus response' in the vertebrate retina, where an omitted component of a periodic pattern predictively elicits robust neuronal activity (Schwartz et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Schwartz et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The brain is a 'predictive machine'.
claims.source: These examples highlight that the brain is a 'predictive machine' (Rao & Ballard 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a general theoretical statement supported by citation.

claims.claim: STMD neurons predict consistency of a selected target's trajectory while suppressing distracters, instead of encoding novelty or the unexpected.
claims.source: However, instead of encoding novelty or the unexpected, STMD neurons predict consistency of a selected target's trajectory, all whilst suppressing distracters.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Direction selectivity is a simple form of prediction.
claims.source: Direction selectivity is, in effect, a simple form of prediction.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual statement based on understanding of direction selectivity.

claims.claim: The Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator provides a nonlinear, facilitated response when an adjacent point is stimulated within a future period.
claims.source: For example, the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator provides a nonlinear, facilitated response when an adjacent point is stimulated within a future period (Hassenstein and Reichardt, 1956).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Hassenstein and Reichardt, 1956.

claims.claim: Direction selective models like the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator cannot explain the observation of a traveling gain modulation that spreads further forward the longer the occlusion.
claims.source: However, such direction selective models cannot explain the observation of a traveling gain modulation that spreads further forward, the longer the occlusion.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the observed phenomena with known models.

claims.claim: Direction selective models cannot account for changes in preferred direction determined by the target's previous direction of travel.
claims.source: Neither can these models account for changes in preferred direction, determined by the target's previous direction of travel.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of standard models compared to observations.

results.result: Dragonfly STMD neurons exhibit a localized 'focus' of enhanced sensitivity just ahead of a moving target's prior path, with over 50% increase in spike rate at the focus center and up to 50% decrease in surrounding locations. This spatial modulation of gain is demonstrated through primer-probe experiments where a preceding target trajectory (primer) alters responses to subsequent test stimuli (probes) at different spatial locations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C18, C19, C33, and C34 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figures 2-3, showing statistically significant spatial modulation (p=0.0007 for enhancement, p=0.005 for suppression, n=9 dragonflies). The 2D receptive field mapping with appropriate controls (probe alone vs. primer+probe) provides robust evidence for the localized focus phenomenon.

results.result: The focus of gain modulation is predictive, spreading forward after temporal delays to account for expected target location. With a 300 ms occlusion, the focus shifts forward in spatial extent (p=0.005, n=7 dragonflies) to the position where the target would have traveled. Direction tuning also shifts to match the prior path, demonstrating trajectory-dependent prediction.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C20, C21, C35, C36, and C42 are well-supported by data in Figures 3B, 3E, 4, and 6. The forward spreading of the focus after delays (statistically significant, p=0.03 for 100 ms vs 300 ms comparison) and direction-dependent facilitation provide strong evidence for predictive mechanisms rather than simple persistence of activity.

results.result: The gain modulation involves a large local increase in contrast sensitivity (>5-fold increase, contrast threshold reduced from 0.071 to 0.013, n=9 dragonflies). Both low and high contrast primers produce similar facilitation effects, suggesting a contrast-invariant 'switch' mechanism rather than activity-dependent gain control. The effect is spatially localized to the focus region.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C52, C53, C54, C56, and C58 are strongly supported by contrast sensitivity experiments in Figure 5. The quantitative measurements show robust increases in contrast gain with appropriate controls (distant primer shows no facilitation). The similarity of effects from low and high contrast primers (Figure 5C,D) supports the inference of a switch-like mechanism, though this interpretation remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The predictive focus can transfer between brain hemispheres. When a primer moves toward the visual midline in the contralateral eye (avoiding binocular overlap), the focus appears in the ipsilateral hemisphere with localized enhancement ahead of the trajectory and suppression at higher elevations. This demonstrates inter-hemispheric transfer of spatially-localized predictive information.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C37, C38, C39, C40, and C41 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3C (n=7 dragonflies, p=0.004 for enhancement, p=0.02 for suppression). The careful experimental design avoiding binocular overlap strengthens the conclusion of inter-hemispheric transfer. However, the mechanistic interpretation (C39, C40) involves inference beyond direct observation. The functional speculation (C41) is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: Direction tuning shifts to match the primer's direction of motion, with all four cardinal direction primers facilitating responses maximally in their respective directions. However, this apparent direction selectivity results from spatial displacement of the focus ahead of the target, not from changes in local motion detector tuning. Probes jumped into the focus center show weaker direction selectivity (b1/b0 ratio 0.32 vs 0.50, p=0.04), and trajectory reversals are strongly inhibited.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C72 are well-supported by direction selectivity experiments in Figures 6-7 (n=9 dragonflies for main experiments, n=5 for jump experiments). The comparison between continuous paths and jumped probes (Figure 7) provides strong evidence that direction selectivity arises from spatial focus displacement rather than changes in underlying motion detectors. The contrast with vertebrate retinal responses (C68) appropriately contextualizes the findings.

results.result: The spatial extent and temporal dynamics of the focus were characterized using instantaneous jumps and pauses. Small jumps (4°) ahead produce rapid facilitated responses, while larger jumps (12-20°) reveal suppression. Facilitation decays slowly at the last seen location (Cohen's d=4.48), and when jumps are matched to occlusion durations, responses are significantly enhanced (Cohen's d=2.0 and 2.32 for 12° and 20° jumps respectively).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 are supported by detailed experiments in Figure 4 (n=8-9 dragonflies). The systematic variation of jump sizes and pause durations with appropriate statistical analyses provides robust characterization of the focus properties. The data convincingly demonstrate both spatial extent and temporal evolution of the predictive modulation.

results.result: Facilitation is observed in earlier-stage small-field (SF) STMD neurons, with primers moving toward the receptive field facilitating probe responses by over 40% (p=0.0004, n=13 dragonflies). Large-field STMDs show even stronger facilitation (>80%, n=11 dragonflies). At least one SF-STMD axon traverses the brain with contralateral arborization, providing anatomical substrate for inter-hemispheric transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by experiments in Figure 8 with appropriate sample sizes and statistical tests. The demonstration of facilitation in SF-STMDs and the anatomical evidence (dye-filled neuron) provide mechanistic insight. However, the inference that SF-STMDs mediate inter-hemispheric transfer (C81) is reasonable but not directly proven—it remains a plausible hypothesis based on anatomy and function.

results.result: Long continuous target trajectories elicit higher overall spiking activity compared to short trajectories at the same spatial locations. Responses build slowly over hundreds of milliseconds (facilitation), but decay rapidly when stimuli end, indicating the effect is not simply due to slow kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 are supported by data in Figure 1 comparing short vs. long trajectories and primer vs. probe conditions. The observation of slow rise but rapid decay (C30) effectively rules out simple temporal integration as an explanation. This establishes the basic phenomenon that motivates the subsequent detailed investigations.

results.result: CSTMD1's excitatory receptive field extends from the dorsal visual midline to the periphery, while targets in the contralateral hemifield generate inhibition, suppressing activity below spontaneous levels (0 spikes/s from spontaneous 11±4 spikes/s).
results.evaluation: Claims C31 and C32 are supported by receptive field mapping data in Figure 1D,E. This characterization of the basic receptive field structure provides essential context for interpreting the dynamic modulation experiments. The measurements are straightforward and well-documented.

results.result: Small backward jumps (6°) over the previously primed path reset responses to unfacilitated levels, while larger backward jumps (12°) reveal potent suppression. This suppression persists for stimuli presented up to 700 ms after the target last traversed that location, indicating long-lasting effects on the surrounding receptive field.
results.evaluation: Claims C43 and C44 are supported by data in Figure 3E. The graded effect of backward jump size and the inference about long-lasting suppression (C44) are reasonable given the experimental timeline. This demonstrates the temporal persistence of the surround suppression component of the focus.

results.result: Following high contrast primers, a hyperpolarizing motion-after-effect (MAE) reaches almost 4 mV and suppresses spiking activity for several hundred milliseconds. This interaction between facilitation and longer-term suppression may be analogous to 'inhibition of return' in human reaction time experiments.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is well-supported by intracellular recordings in Figure 5D,E showing the MAE. However, C61's analogy to inhibition of return is speculative—while the comparison is interesting and potentially valid, it lacks direct experimental support. The MAE observation itself is solid, but the functional interpretation remains uncertain.

results.result: Direction selectivity (vector magnitude) is established more rapidly than the gain in facilitated responses over a target's developing trajectory. This rapid emergence of directional tuning suggests the modulation may assist trajectory anticipation by promoting expectation of continued motion.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is supported by data in Figure 7D showing faster establishment of direction selectivity. However, C74's interpretation about assisting anticipation is speculative—while plausible given the data, it represents a functional hypothesis rather than a directly tested mechanism. The observation is solid but the interpretation requires further validation.

results.result: The reduction in slope of the contrast sensitivity function would reduce overall response variance to changes in the contrast of the selected target, a phenomenon also observed in humans.
results.evaluation: Claim C57 is supported by the shape of the contrast sensitivity function in Figure 5C and comparison with human studies (Avidan et al., 2002). The inference about reduced variance is mathematically sound given the shallower slope at high contrasts. This represents a reasonable functional interpretation of the observed gain modulation properties.

results.result: A distant primer displaced 20° to the side of the probe does not evoke facilitation of the contrast sensitivity function, demonstrating spatial specificity of the gain modulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by control experiments in Figure 5C (yellow line). This negative control is essential for demonstrating that the facilitation is spatially localized rather than a global arousal effect. The control is well-designed and appropriately executed.

results.result: CSTMD1 is only weakly direction-selective for prolonged paths, with weak preference for progressive motion upwards and away from the midline. Probe responses alone are both weak and weakly direction selective.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are supported by baseline characterization in Figure 6C and prior work (Nordström et al., 2011). This establishes the baseline weak direction selectivity that is then dramatically altered by primers, making the primer-induced changes more striking. The characterization is straightforward and well-documented.

results.result: A neuron's receptive field is a dynamic representation of spatial and temporal context, not just stimulus selectivity. This modulation represents anticipatory coding—a more complex influence of history than simple adaptation, sensitization, habituation or fatigue. STMD neurons predict consistency of a selected target's trajectory while suppressing distracters.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C83, and C86 represent interpretive conclusions drawn from the collective experimental results. These interpretations are well-supported by the data showing spatial localization, temporal dynamics, direction dependence, and contrast invariance. The distinction from simpler mechanisms (adaptation, etc.) is justified by the complexity of the observed phenomena. These are appropriate high-level conclusions from the work.

results.result: The observed phenomena cannot be explained by standard direction-selective models like the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator. These models cannot account for: traveling gain modulation spreading with occlusion duration, changes in preferred direction matching prior trajectory, contrast-invariant switching, large suppressive surrounds, or the larger spatial (tens of degrees) and temporal (hundreds of milliseconds) scales. The inter-hemispheric transfer is more reminiscent of higher-order attentional networks than local motion encoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 provide critical analysis distinguishing the observed mechanisms from standard motion detection models. The arguments are logically sound and well-supported by the experimental observations. The comparison with known models and the identification of features incompatible with those models strengthens the novelty claims. The interpretation about higher-order processing (C93) is reasonable given the complexity and scale of the effects.

results.result: The >400% increase in contrast sensitivity is consistent with but significantly larger than vertebrate attention studies (humans ~40% increase, macaque V4 ~51% increase). The facilitation in CSTMD1 reveals a combination of both contrast gain and response gain modulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 appropriately contextualize the findings within the broader attention literature. The comparisons with vertebrate studies (Carrasco et al., 2000; Reynolds et al., 2000) are accurate, and the observation that dragonfly effects are larger is well-supported by the data. The interpretation of combined contrast and response gain (C97) from Figure 5C is reasonable given the shape of the function.

results.result: In vertebrate retina, adaptation and sensitization allow ganglion cells to track moving targets and anticipate straight-line motion, with trajectory reversals eliciting synchronous bursts. However, this does not extrapolate future locations—the last observed location remains sensitized. In contrast, human observers show improved sensitivity at extrapolated forward locations during occlusions, indicating additional processing beyond the retina.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C12 accurately summarize prior work on vertebrate motion processing (Berry et al., 1999; Kastner and Baccus, 2013; Schwartz et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2014; Watamaniuk and McKee, 1995). These claims provide appropriate context for the dragonfly findings. The citations appear accurate and the distinctions drawn between retinal and behavioral levels are valid.

results.result: STMD neurons in dragonfly Hemicordulia tau are tuned to target size, velocity, and contrast. CSTMD1 responds selectively to small moving targets even in natural scenes and exhibits winner-takes-all selective attention, responding to one target while completely ignoring distracters.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 accurately summarize prior characterization of STMD neurons from the authors' previous work (O'Carroll 1993; Wiederman et al., 2008, 2011, 2013). These claims establish the baseline properties of the neurons being studied and are well-supported by the cited literature. This background is essential for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: Small-field STMDs are located at earlier visual processing stages than CSTMD1, with inputs in the outer lobula (analogous to mammalian primary visual cortex). They have properties similar to end-stopped (hypercomplex) cells and are modulated by contextual stimuli outside their classical receptive field.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 accurately describe SF-STMD properties based on prior work (Barnett et al., 2007; Okamura and Strausfeld, 2007; O'Carroll 1993; Nordström and O'Carroll, 2009; Polat et al., 1998). These claims provide important context for understanding the hierarchical organization and the potential mechanisms underlying the observed effects. The citations appear accurate.

results.result: Many animals detect moving objects in clutter, a complex task for small targets with weak contrast. Dragonflies capture prey in visual clutter using winner-takes-all selection. In other animals, inhibitory circuits drive salient stimulus selection and attention is evidenced by contrast gain modulation. How prediction relates to selection is unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C17 provide general background on visual motion detection, attention, and prediction across species. These are accurate statements of established knowledge supported by appropriate citations (Corbet, 1999; Wiederman and O'Carroll, 2013; Mysore and Knudsen, 2013; Moran and Desimone, 1985; Reynolds et al., 2000; Zirnsak et al., 2014). This background appropriately motivates the study.

results.result: The gain modulation may indicate a 'switch' process rather than activity-dependent gain control. The modulation could be inherent to prediction or result from the primer acting as an attentional cue. The predictive focus may 'lock on' to single targets while suppressing distracters, potentially explaining winner-takes-all behavior through positive feedback.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C98, and C100 are explicitly speculative (noted as SPECULATION in evidence_type). While these hypotheses are reasonable given the data (contrast-invariant effects, winner-takes-all behavior), they lack direct experimental support. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than conclusions. Further experiments would be needed to distinguish between these mechanistic alternatives.

results.result: The 'omitted stimulus response' in vertebrate retina demonstrates predictive processing. The brain is a 'predictive machine.' Direction selectivity is a simple form of prediction, as exemplified by the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator providing facilitated responses when adjacent points are stimulated within a future period.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C85, C87, and C88 provide theoretical context from prior work (Schwartz et al., 2007; Rao & Ballard 1999; Hassenstein and Reichardt, 1956). These are accurate statements of established concepts in neuroscience and provide appropriate framing for the current findings. The citations appear accurate and the conceptual framework is sound.

results.result: CSTMD1 selectively attends to one target when presented with competing stimuli, completely ignoring distracters (from prior work). The dragonfly is a sophisticated yet tractable model for investigating neuronal mechanisms of prediction and selective attention.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 accurately cites prior work (Wiederman and O'Carroll, 2013) establishing winner-takes-all behavior. Claim C101 is a reasonable concluding statement about the value of the model system, supported by the complexity of mechanisms revealed in the current study. The dragonfly does appear to offer advantages for studying these phenomena given the accessibility for in vivo recordings.

results.result: Methodological details: Recordings from 63 wild-caught male Hemicordulia tau dragonflies using intracellular electrodes (50-150 MΩ resistance) inserted into the proximal lobula complex. CSTMD1 identified by characteristic receptive field, tuning, and action potentials. Visual stimuli presented on LCD monitors (≥120 Hz) with 1.5°×1.5° black squares at 40°/s. Minimum 7 s inter-trial intervals to avoid habituation.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C107 describe standard methodological details that are clearly stated in the Materials and Methods section. The sample size (n=63 dragonflies total), electrode specifications, neuron identification criteria, stimulus parameters, and experimental design details are all appropriate and well-documented. These methods are suitable for the experiments performed.
